246.title: Al-Fattah, the Opener
246.hook: the Opener, of doors, of hearts, of ways out
246.howItsDone: Many Muslims say Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik, O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy, when entering a mosque, and call on al-Fattah when a matter is stuck, asking for an opening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Razzaq: the birds out hungry and back full, and the camel tied. Your line was provided for. Before a meal, did you pause for one breath of thanks? Day two hundred forty-six.

Remember Hudaybiyyah, eleven days ago? The treaty where the name ar-Rahman was struck from the first line. The rest of that treaty felt worse. The Muslims had come to visit the Ka'ba and were sent home without reaching it. Some of the terms looked one-sided. Many companions were deeply upset; Umar, Bukhari records, went to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asking why they should accept such terms. They rode back toward Medina with their heads down. And on the way, a surah came down, and its first line called that treaty a clear victory. The Arabic word for victory there is the same word as opening. Today: Al-Fattah, the Opener.
screen: `SENT HOME FROM MECCA.` → `A TREATY THAT FELT LIKE A LOSS.` → `CALLED A CLEAR VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Inna fatahna laka fathan mubina. The first line of Surah al-Fath: We have opened for you a clear opening, a clear victory. The root is f-t-h, to open. It gives miftah, a key. It gives fath, an opening, and a victory, because a victory is a way through. And it gives the name of the first surah you learned: al-Fatiha, the opening. The treaty that looked like a door slamming turned out to be a door opening: two years of peace, in which, historians say, more people entered Islam than in all the years before. Al-Fattah is the one who opens. The Qur'an uses the name in Surah Saba', where it has a second shade: our Lord will bring us together, then He will open between us with truth, and He is al-Fattah, al-'Alim, the Opener, the All-Knowing. Here opening means judging: laying a dispute open so the truth is seen. In Surah Fatir, whatever mercy Allah opens for people, no one can hold back; and whatever He holds back, no one can release. And in al-An'am: with Him are the keys of the unseen. So the name covers every kind of stuck: a locked door, a locked-up heart, a dispute no one can settle, a way out when you can't see one. When Muslims enter a mosque, many say words the Prophet taught, recorded by Muslim: O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy. The one entering asks; the opening is left to al-Fattah.
screen: `FATH — AN OPENING, A VICTORY.` · `MIFTAH, FATH, AL-FATIHA.` · `OPENING THE TRUTH BETWEEN PEOPLE.` · `THE KEYS OF THE UNSEEN.` · then, large: `THE OPENER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and name one thing in your life that feels stuck. A conversation that goes nowhere. A job search. A friendship gone cold. Something in you that won't budge. Picture it as a closed door. Don't push on it. Just stand in front of it and breathe. Notice that you don't hold the key, and let that be a relief instead of a fear. If you pray, you can ask Allah, al-Fattah, to open it, or to open another way you haven't seen. The bell holds the time.
Al-Fattah. The Opener, of doors, hearts and ways out, and the one who opens the truth between people. Today's word.
Your line: the opener. Today, each time you open a door, say the word to yourself, and remember the one stuck thing you named. Day two hundred forty-six.

al-Fatiha and al-Fattah share a root

what it means: the Opener of doors, hearts and ways out, and the one who opens the truth between people.

247.title: Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing
247.hook: the All-Knowing, who knows what the heart hides
247.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a, personal prayer, in any language and at any time, often quietly, following the example of prophets like Zakariyya; many find the night, and the prostration of the prayer, the most natural times to say what they have told no one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Fattah: the treaty that felt like a loss and was called a clear opening. Your line was the opener. What stuck thing did you name at the door? Day two hundred forty-seven.

Everyone carries at least one thing they've never said out loud. A fear. A hope that feels too big or too silly. Something they did. Something that was done to them. It sits in a back room of the heart, and we get very good at walking past the door. Surah Maryam begins with an old man doing the opposite. Zakariyya, a prophet and a priest, his hair gone white, his bones weak, his wife unable to have children for all these years. At night, alone, he calls on his Lord, the surah says, with a hidden call, a secret one. He says the thing he's never said. Today: Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing.
screen: `ONE THING NEVER SAID OUT LOUD.` → `AN OLD MAN, AT NIGHT, ALONE.` → `A HIDDEN CALL.`

segments.voice: What Zakariyya says is simple and raw: my bones have grown weak, my head is shining with gray, and I have never been disappointed in calling on You. I want someone to carry on after me. Then he waits. We'll see in a moment what happens. First, the name. Al-'Alim comes from the root '-l-m, to know. It gives 'ilm, knowledge; 'ulama', scholars; mu'allim, a teacher. By common counts, the name appears in the Qur'an more than a hundred and fifty times, often at the end of a verse, like a signature: and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. What does He know? Everything, the Qur'an says, but it keeps pointing at the small and the hidden. In al-An'am, not a leaf falls but He knows it. In Ta Ha, if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is even more hidden. In al-Mulk: He knows what is in the breasts; should He not know, the one who created? And in Surah Qaf, in Pickthall's words: We verily created man and We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein. So why did Zakariyya say it at all, if Allah already knew? Muslims say du'a isn't news delivered to Allah. It's the servant turning toward the one who already knows, and being changed by the turning. Zakariyya's hidden call was answered with glad news: a son, Yahya, John, a name the surah says was given to no one before him. The back room of the heart has always had a listener.
screen: `MY BONES HAVE GROWN WEAK.` · `'-L-M — TO KNOW.` · `NEARER THAN THE JUGULAR VEIN.` · `DU'A IS TURNING, NOT INFORMING.` · then, large: `HE ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit somewhere you won't be interrupted. Let your breath slow. Now let the back-room thing come forward, the one you haven't said to anyone. You don't need to fix it or explain it. If you pray, you can tell Allah, silently, in plain words, the way Zakariyya did. If you don't pray, you can simply say it to yourself, honestly, in the quiet, and let it be known by you. Then rest, and notice what it's like for the thing to be said and not hidden. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Alim. The All-Knowing, who knows the leaf that falls, the secret and what's more hidden still: what the heart hides. Today's word.
Your line: he already knows. Today, when you're tempted to hide something or perform for someone, remember there's nothing to perform. Day two hundred forty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: God knows everything, like a database.
what it means: the one who knows the hidden, the whisper of the soul, and is nearer than the jugular vein.
what a scholar hears: '-l-m gives 'ilm, 'ulama', mu'allim; the name recurs, by common counts, over a hundred and fifty times; 50:16, 20:7, 67:13–14; Zakariyya's nida' khafi in 19:3.

248.title: As-Sami' and al-Basir
248.hook: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, who hears whispers and sees the ant
248.howItsDone: Muslims call on God as as-Sami' and al-Basir in private du'a, often quietly or silently, and many say after rising from bowing in prayer that God hears the one who praises him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, who knows what the heart hides. Your line was he already knows. Did you tell him the thing you'd told no one? Day two hundred forty-eight.

A woman in Medina has a problem at home, and it's a bad one. Her husband has said an old Arabian oath that leaves her neither married nor free. She comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she argues. She pleads. She complains, out loud, to God. His wife Aisha is in the same room, and she said later that she could not even hear all of what the woman was saying. It was that low, that close. And then verses came down that begin: God has heard the words of the woman who argued with you about her husband. The person in the room missed some of it. The one she was really talking to missed none of it. Today, two names that go together: the One who hears, and the One who sees.
screen: `A WOMAN ARGUES HER CASE.` → `AISHA CAN'T HEAR IT ALL.` → `GOD HAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: As-Sami': the All-Hearing, from sam', hearing. Al-Basir: the All-Seeing, from basar, sight. In the Qur'an they very often come as a pair, at the end of a verse, like two notes of one chord. One verse puts it this way, in Pickthall's old translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Notice what that line does. First it says nothing is like him. Then it uses two words we use about ourselves. Muslim scholars read it as a guard rail: God hears and sees, truly, but not with ears and eyes like ours, and not the way we do. Our hearing gets tired. His doesn't. Our sight needs light. His doesn't. There's a saying often repeated in Muslim teaching, that God sees a black ant on a black stone on a moonless night. It's a picture, not a verse, but it makes the point: nothing is too small or too dark. And the pair isn't only about being watched. When Moses and Aaron are sent to face Pharaoh, they're afraid, and God tells them not to fear: "Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing." That's comfort, not surveillance. The woman in Medina is the same lesson told as a story. She had no lawyer, no power, no loud voice. She had a complaint whispered in a corner, and the chapter she's remembered in is named for her: al-Mujadilah, the woman who argues. The Prophet taught that when people call on God, they're not calling someone deaf or far away. Heard. Seen. Even the whisper.
screen: `SAMI' — HEARING. BASIR — SEEING.` · `NOTHING IS LIKE HIM.` · `I AM WITH YOU, HEARING AND SEEING.` · `THE WOMAN WHO ARGUES.` · then, large: `HEARD. SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: whisper a du'a. Sit, and let the room go quiet. Think of one thing you want, or one thing that hurts, and say it so softly nobody near you could catch it. In your own words, in any language. If you pray, you can speak it to God, as quietly as the woman in Medina. If you don't, just let yourself say it at all, and notice how different it feels to say a thing than to only think it. Then sit in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
As-Sami' and al-Basir. The All-Hearing and the All-Seeing, two names that travel together through the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: heard, seen. Today, when you feel overlooked, in a meeting, a group chat, a kitchen, say those two words to yourself once. Day two hundred forty-eight.

fork.reveal: she argued and complained to God, so quietly Aisha missed some of it, and a whole surah opens with God has heard her.

original.note: Arabic: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. from sam' (hearing) and basar (sight).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is watching you.
what it means: nothing is too quiet to be heard or too small to be seen, and the Qur'an mostly says it as comfort.

249.title: Al-Latif, the Subtle
249.hook: the Subtle, the Gentle, who works in ways too fine to see
249.howItsDone: Many Muslims call on God as ya Latif in times of worry, and some repeat the name as a dhikr, asking for gentleness in something hard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, As-Sami' and al-Basir, the All-Hearing and the All-Seeing. Your line was heard, seen. Did you whisper something, and feel it land? Day two hundred forty-nine.

Think back over a stretch of your life that went wrong in a way you'd never have chosen. The job that fell through. The move you didn't want. The friend who left. And then, years later, notice where you are, and how many good things in your life only happened because of that wrong turn. Nobody announced it at the time. There was no sign on the road. It just turned out, slowly, that something was being worked in a way too fine to see from inside. The Qur'an has a man who lived exactly that, at the scale of a whole life. And when he finally looks back on it, he reaches for one name. Today: Al-Latif.
screen: `THE WRONG TURN.` → `YEARS LATER, LOOKING BACK.` → `ONE NAME FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Al-Latif comes from a root, l-t-f, that holds two meanings at once. One is fine, delicate, subtle, too small or too thin to see. The other is gentle, kind, tender. Arabic doesn't make you choose. A latif breeze is soft. A latif touch is careful. So the name means the One who is subtle and the One who is gentle, and scholars say the two are joined: his kindness reaches you by paths so fine you don't notice them. One verse puts the name right next to sight. In Pickthall's translation: "Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision. He is the Subtile, the Aware." Subtile is an old spelling of subtle. You can't see him; he sees all the way in. Now the man. Yusuf, Joseph. Thrown in a well by his brothers. Sold as a slave. Falsely accused. Years in prison. Every step looks like a step down. At the end of his surah, he's a minister of Egypt, his parents and brothers are bowing before him, and his childhood dream has come true. He doesn't say, I earned this, or even, look how it all worked out. He says, in the Qur'an's words, that his Lord is latif to whom he wills: gentle, working in fine ways toward what he intends. The well, the prison, the long wait, and it was gentleness the whole time, just too fine to see from the bottom of the well. That's the name. Not that nothing hurts. Yusuf's story hurts for a long time. But that a gentle hand can be at work inside the part that hurts.
screen: `L-T-F — FINE, AND GENTLE.` · `VISION COMPREHENDETH HIM NOT.` · `THE WELL, THE PRISON, THE WAIT.` · `MY LORD IS LATIF.` · then, large: `GENTLE BEYOND SEEING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a gentle turn in your week. Sit, and go back over the last seven days slowly. Look for something small that went better than it might have. A conversation that softened. A delay that turned out to help. Someone who texted at the right moment. Don't look for miracles, look for fine things, the kind you'd normally walk past. When you find one, stay with it. If you pray, you can call God by this name, ya Latif. If not, just let yourself be grateful for it. The bell holds the time.
Al-Latif. The Subtle and the Gentle at once: kindness that works in ways too fine to see. Today's word.
Your line: gentle beyond seeing. Today, when something goes a little sideways, hold off on calling it bad for an hour, and see what it turns into. Day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: Al-Halim, the Forbearing
250.hook: the Forbearing, who doesn't rush to punish
250.howItsDone: Muslims name God as al-Halim, often alongside al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, and many take the Prophet's advice not to get angry as a daily discipline, pausing, sitting down or making wudu when anger rises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Latif, the Subtle and the Gentle. Your line was gentle beyond seeing. Did something go sideways and turn out better than you feared? Day two hundred fifty.

Somebody cuts you off in traffic. Your thumb is already on the horn. A message lands in the group chat that's clearly about you, and your reply is half typed before you've finished reading. Anger is fast. It's one of the fastest things a person has. And the people we end up admiring most are often the ones who have a gap in them, a pause between the sting and the answer. You say something awful to them, and they wait, and they don't hand it back. Old Arabia had a word for that pause, and it prized it in its chiefs long before Islam. The Qur'an takes that word and makes it a name of God. Today: Al-Halim.
screen: `THUMB ON THE HORN.` → `THE PAUSE BEFORE THE ANSWER.` → `A NAME FOR THE PAUSE.`

segments.voice: Al-Halim comes from hilm. In old Arabia, hilm was the great virtue of a leader: calm, self-control, the power to hold back when you could strike. Its opposite was jahl. We usually translate jahl as ignorance, but in the old poems it often means hot-headedness, the man who flies off the handle and starts a feud over an insult. So when the Qur'an calls God al-Halim, it means the One who sees every wrong, has all the power to answer it at once, and doesn't rush. The Qur'an says it plainly: if God took people to task right away for everything they earned, he wouldn't leave a single creature walking on the earth. Instead, he gives time. Time to notice. Time to turn around. Muslims hear forbearance in that delay, not indifference: al-Halim sees, and waits, because the waiting leaves the door open. The name often sits beside forgiving. First he holds back; then he forgives. And hilm is a name a person can grow into. The Qur'an calls Abraham halim. And when a chief named al-Ashajj came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with his people, the Prophet told him, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, that he had two qualities God loves: hilm, forbearance, and anah, taking your time. Another man asked the Prophet for advice, and was told, don't get angry, and when he asked again, the same answer, again. Not that anger never comes. That it doesn't get to drive.
screen: `HILM — THE CHIEF'S CALM.` · `JAHL — THE HOT HEAD.` · `HE SEES, AND GIVES TIME.` · `TWO QUALITIES GOD LOVES.` · then, large: `SLOW TO ANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait before reacting today, and rehearse it now. Sit, and bring back a moment from this week when something stung. Feel how fast the answer wanted to come. Now, in your mind, put a gap there. One slow breath in. One slow breath out. Then, only then, picture what you'd say. Notice whether it's different. Run it once more with a different moment. If you pray, you can ask God, al-Halim, for a little of his hilm. The bell holds the time.
Al-Halim. The Forbearing: the One who sees every wrong, holds all the power, and doesn't rush to punish. Today's word.
Your line: slow to anger. Today, the next time something stings, take one breath before you answer, just one, and see what comes out instead. Day two hundred fifty.

251.title: Al-Wadud, the Loving
251.hook: the Loving, whose love is steady and shown
251.howItsDone: Muslims call on God as al-Wadud in du'a, and many understand love for others as something shown in deeds: gifts, visits, help, and a hadith that says to give gifts to one another so love grows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Halim, the Forbearing, who doesn't rush to punish. Your line was slow to anger. Did you catch one breath between the sting and the answer? Day two hundred fifty-one.

Some people never say I love you. A father who gets up at five to scrape the ice off your windshield before you're awake. A grandmother who remembers you hate onions and quietly picks them out of your plate for thirty years. A friend who shows up to help you move and doesn't mention it again. You know the love, not because anyone said it, but because it keeps showing up, in the same shape, over and over. Arabic has more than one word for love, and one of them is exactly this: love that shows. Love you can see in what it does. The Qur'an uses it as a name of God. Today: Al-Wadud.
screen: `ICE SCRAPED OFF THE WINDSHIELD.` → `NO ONIONS, FOR THIRTY YEARS.` → `LOVE THAT SHOWS.`

segments.voice: You first met this name at Al-Buruj, on day two hundred five, sitting right after the Forgiving. Today, among the names, follow where that love goes. Start with the word. Arabic's everyday word for love is hubb. Wudd is different. Scholars of the language describe it as love that comes out: affection you can see, steady, like the ice scraper at five a.m. So al-Wadud is not only the One who loves, but the One whose love keeps showing. And the Qur'an uses the same word for something that happens between people. In Surah Maryam it says that for those who believe and do good, the Merciful will appoint wudd, love. Not a reward stored away for later. Love set down among them, here. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari shows how that love travels. When God loves a servant, He calls the angel Jibril and tells him: I love this person, so love them. Jibril loves them, and calls out to the people of heaven, and they love them. And then acceptance is set down for them on the earth. You've probably met someone like that: people trust them before they know why. So the name runs in two directions. Love comes down, steady and shown. And a person can pass it on by making love visible. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put it in the most ordinary terms, in a saying collected by al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad: give gifts to one another, and you will love one another. Not a speech. A deed. That's how wudd gets passed along.
screen: `WUDD — LOVE THAT SHOWS.` · `LOVE SET DOWN AMONG PEOPLE.` · `JIBRIL, THEN HEAVEN, THEN EARTH.` · `LOVE MADE VISIBLE IN DEEDS.` · then, large: `LOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show love to someone in a deed. Sit for a moment and let a face come to mind, someone who'd never guess you're thinking of them. Then choose one small thing you could do for them today. Not a speech. A deed. Make the tea. Send the photo. Fix the thing that's been broken. Picture yourself doing it. And, if you pray, you can call on God as al-Wadud, the Loving. Then just sit, and let yourself be loved for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Al-Wadud. The Loving: love that is steady, and shown, not only felt. Today's word.
Your line: loved. Today, do the one deed you pictured, and don't mention it. Let it speak for itself. Day two hundred fifty-one.

what a scholar hears: wudd, not hubb: lexicographers describe it as affection made visible. as a name it appears at 11:90 and 85:14; at 19:96 the same word is the love set among believers.

252.title: Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative
252.hook: the Appreciative, who rewards the smallest good
252.howItsDone: Many Muslims take the hadith of the thorny branch literally and clear obstacles from paths and roads, and the Prophet counted removing harm from the road as a branch of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Wadud, the Loving, whose love is shown. Your line was loved. Did you do the deed, and keep quiet about it? Day two hundred fifty-two, the end of a week.

You held a door. You wiped the counter someone else left sticky. You moved the scooter off the sidewalk so the next person with a stroller wouldn't have to. Nobody saw. Nobody said thanks. And a small voice in you said: well, that didn't count. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told a story about a man walking down a road who found a thorny branch lying across it. He moved it out of the way, so it wouldn't hurt anyone. That's the whole deed. And the hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says God thanked him for it, and forgave him. God thanked him. For a branch. Today, the name behind that word: Ash-Shakur.
screen: `NOBODY SAW.` → `A THORNY BRANCH ON THE ROAD.` → `GOD THANKED HIM.`

segments.voice: Ash-Shakur comes from shukr, the word for thanks we met back at the start of the path. When a person has shukr, they're grateful. But what does it mean for God to be shakur? He doesn't need anything from us. Scholars explain it this way: God's shukr is appreciation. He notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. A branch moved, a whole life forgiven. That's the scale. The Qur'an puts it in two lines that many Muslims know by heart. In Pickthall's translation: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then." An atom's weight. In the Arabic it's a dharrah, a speck, some say the tiniest ant. Nothing is too small to be seen, and then answered. And the Prophet backed it up in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: don't look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. A smile is on the list. Now look back at this week, because every name has pointed here. Al-Fattah opened. Al-'Alim knew what the heart hides. As-Sami' and al-Basir heard the whisper and saw the ant. Al-Latif worked too finely to see. Al-Halim held back. Al-Wadud loved, and showed it. And Ash-Shakur notices the smallest thing you did, and doesn't let it disappear. Seven names, one picture: nothing about you is too small, too quiet, or too hidden to count.
screen: `SHUKR — THANKS, FROM GOD.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD.` · `EVEN A CHEERFUL FACE.` · `SEVEN NAMES THIS WEEK.` · then, large: `NOTHING SMALL IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone for something tiny. Sit, and go back over today. Find the smallest kind thing anyone did for you. The barista who remembered your name. The coworker who refilled the printer. The kid who put their plate in the sink without being asked. Choose one. Picture the moment you'll thank them, and exactly what you'll say, naming the small thing, so they know it was seen. If you pray, you can thank God for it too. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Shakur. The Appreciative: the One who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. Today's word.
Your line: nothing small is lost. Today, thank that one person, out loud, for the tiny thing. Day two hundred fifty-two.

fork.reveal: the man in the hadith moved it, and God thanked him and forgave him. the smallest deed, answered at full size.

original.note: Arabic: the Appreciative. from shukr, thanks: here, the One who rewards small good richly.

trapdoor: what you thought: we're supposed to thank God.
what it means: God is the Appreciative one, who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size.
what a scholar hears: the hadith uses the verb shakara of God: he thanked the man. scholars read God's shukr as reward, never as need.
